title: Two American Airlines Jets Share Same Flight Number in Close Call Over Phoenix
excerpt: A veteran air traffic controller spotted the identical call signs and guided both Boeing 737s safely apart as the FAA opens an investigation into the rare incident near Phoenix Sky Harbor.
body:
• Two American Airlines Boeing 737s operated simultaneously in Phoenix airspace using the identical flight number AA2482, creating a potentially dangerous situation shortly after midnight on August 14
  • A veteran air traffic controller with 25 years of experience identified the duplicate call sign and safely guided both aircraft apart, distinguishing them as "American 2482 on the arrival" and "American 2482 on the departure"
  • The duplicate arose after weather delays in Chicago prompted the airline to assign a second aircraft in Phoenix the same flight number for the return leg
  • The FAA has confirmed it is investigating the incident, while American Airlines says required separation was maintained throughout

How Two Jets Ended Up Sharing a Call Sign

Two American Airlines passenger jets flew through Phoenix airspace with the same flight number in the early hours of August 14, a rare and potentially hazardous situation that was averted by an alert air traffic controller at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

https://x.com/flightradar24/status/2088309221423038875

Under normal operations, a single aircraft flies back and forth on American Airlines Flight 2482 between Chicago O'Hare International Airport and Phoenix. But when weather delays held up the Chicago-bound departure, the airline dispatched a second plane already on the ground in Phoenix to cover the return leg — assigning it the same Flight 2482 designation, according to the Associated Press, which first reported the incident.

The result: two Boeing 737s converging in the same airspace under an identical call sign, a scenario that strips air traffic controllers of their primary tool for distinguishing and directing individual aircraft.

Controller's Quick Thinking Averts Crisis

Audio recordings posted on LiveATC.net capture the controller improvising on the fly, referring to the two planes as "American 2482 on the arrival" and "American 2482 on the departure" to keep both pilots oriented.

"I've been working air traffic for 25 years. I've never seen two aircraft pretty much merge with the same call sign. That's pretty incredible."

— Air traffic controller, Phoenix Sky Harbor

The controller's actions kept the arriving aircraft safely above the departing one, maintaining required separation throughout the encounter. A pilot on the inbound flight praised the controller's handling of the situation, to which the controller responded: "Hey no problem — I'm glad it all worked out there. It could have been disastrous. But I'm glad it all worked out."

Airlines and FAA Respond

American Airlines confirmed it is reviewing the incident. "The diligence and professionalism of air traffic controllers and our pilots ensured required separation was always maintained and the issue was identified and addressed," spokesperson Gianna Urgo said in a statement. "Both flights continued safely and without incident."

The Federal Aviation Administration separately confirmed its investigation. "American Airlines Flight 2482 was descending for Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport when another American Airlines flight departed using the same flight number," FAA spokesperson Kelly Lamp said. "Air traffic control recognized the identical call signs and made sure the aircraft maintained the required separation."

Phoenix Sky Harbor spokesperson Ashley Meza declined to comment on the incident, deferring to American Airlines.

A Rare but Known Risk in Aviation

Duplicate call signs are an acknowledged hazard in aviation. The FAA's own controller handbook requires controllers to alert pilots when similar-sounding call signs are on the same frequency. The situation becomes far more dangerous when the call signs are not merely similar but identical, as occurred here.

The incident comes amid heightened scrutiny of U.S. aviation safety. Earlier this summer, two passenger jets nearly collided at Boston Logan International Airport after an air traffic controller lost track of which aircraft he had cleared for takeoff. The FAA has recorded four serious runway incursions so far in 2026, down from 21 in 2023, but close calls continue to draw attention to staffing shortages and aging infrastructure in the nation's air traffic control system.

What Happens Next

The FAA has not provided a timeline for when its investigative report will be completed. The incident is likely to raise questions about airline operational procedures during irregular operations — specifically, how substitute aircraft are assigned flight numbers and whether safeguards exist to prevent duplicate call signs from entering the same airspace.

No passengers were harmed, and both flights completed their journeys without further incident.
nri_angle: The incident on a major domestic route between Chicago and Phoenix — two cities with large Indian-American populations — highlights ongoing aviation safety concerns for frequent U.S. air travelers.
